text.content: Desi Atta Company is the first food collective in India to introduce a wide range of flours and flour-based ready-mixes from ancient Indian grains, millets & pulses. Their vision is to create a community of people who love to cook traditional and experimental dishes with flour. These ready-mixes and unique flours are only available offline, and hence a website to cater for the market, which is rich in delicacies surrounding cultural festivities/festivals.

text.content: The Problem

rich_text.plain_text: The Problem

text.content: Landmark has decided to build a new and independent fashion e-commerce app. This app shows a limited customer set of products (approx. 500), but the key differentiator is that customers can get these products on the same day for a trial (less than 2 hours). The customer has to pay a nominal fee of 7 AED per product as a trial fee (Which has to be paid upfront. Cash on Delivery is not allowed for trial fee payment). Once delivered, the customer can try all the clothes ordered and decide to buy or reject each product. Customers will have 30 minutes to try all the products while the delivery guy waits. If the customer chooses to buy a product (let’s assume the selling price is 100 AED), the trial fee is waived and adjusted in the product cost. The customer can then pay the changed amount (AED 93) online on the app or via cash to the delivery guy. The rejected items will return to the delivery guy.

text.content: The Danger of Data Without Understanding

rich_text.plain_text: The Danger of Data Without Understanding

text.content: AI excels at identifying what users are doing, but it often struggles to explain why they are doing it. For example, an AI algorithm might identify that users are abandoning a checkout process at a specific step. It can even suggest potential solutions, such as simplifying the form or offering a discount. However, it may not be able to tell you why users are abandoning the process. Are they concerned about security? Are they confused by the shipping options? Are they simply distracted?

text.content: The "stack" of a product is its collection of interdependent parts. Its environment is vast and intricate. Among the best analogies I’ve come across from The Software Guild is to picture the IT stack as a burger. A burger must have specific ingredients, but the rest of the sandwich can be customised to the eater’s preferences. The burger in your product might have onions on it, or it might not. The patties were made by one programmer and the cheese by another. Many technologies may make up the stack used by your design team. text.content: Planning a sitemap

A sitemap is essentially a map or directory of your website's pages, providing a hierarchical overview of its structure. It serves as a guide for search engine crawlers and users, enabling them to navigate through the site's content more efficiently. There are two main types of sitemaps: HTML and XML. While XML sitemaps are primarily intended for search engines, HTML sitemaps cater to both search engines and human visitors.

text.content: What Sets Your Brand Apart?

text.content: To stand out in a crowded marketplace, you must identify what makes your brand unique and differentiates it from competitors. Ask yourself what value proposition your brand offers. By understanding your unique selling points, you can effectively communicate your brand's value to your target audience and carve out a distinctive position in the market.

By putting users first, companies can create products that are intuitive, useful, and delightful to use.

text.content: In today's digital landscape, the success of a business hinges on providing exceptional user experiences (UX) and customer experiences (CX). While UX primarily focuses on designing user-friendly interfaces, CX encompasses the overall journey and interactions a customer has with a brand. However, the lines between the two are blurring as businesses realize the importance of integrating these two disciplines. In this blog, we'll delve into the intersection of UX and CX, explore their synergies, and provide insights and examples from the industry.

rich_text.plain_text: In today's digital landscape, the success of a business hinges on providing exceptional user experiences (UX) and customer experiences (CX). While UX primarily focuses on designing user-friendly interfaces, CX encompasses the overall journey and interactions a customer has with a brand. However, the lines between the two are blurring as businesses realize the importance of integrating these two disciplines. In this blog, we'll delve into the intersection of UX and CX, explore their synergies, and provide insights and examples from the industry.

text.content: Customer experience encompasses the entire journey a customer has with a brand, including interactions across various touchpoints (website, app, customer service, etc.). CX focuses on building strong emotional connections, meeting customer expectations, and fostering loyalty.

text.content: Mapping the Journey Together

rich_text.plain_text: Mapping the Journey Together

text.content: A practical starting point for aligning UX and CX is a shared journey map. Bring together the people who own each touchpoint, from product and design to marketing, sales and support, and map the steps a customer actually takes, not the steps the organization assumes they take. Mark where the product experience ends and the wider customer experience begins, and pay close attention to those handoff points. They are often where friction hides, because no single team owns them.

text.content: Shared Metrics for UX and CX

rich_text.plain_text: Shared Metrics for UX and CX

text.content: UX teams often measure task success, error rates and usability scores, while CX teams track satisfaction, loyalty and retention. Looked at separately, these numbers can tell different stories. Looked at together, they show cause and effect: a confusing checkout flow shows up first in usability testing and later in support tickets and churn. Agreeing on a small set of shared measures helps both teams see how a change in one area affects the other.

text.content: Getting Started

rich_text.plain_text: Getting Started

text.content: Organizations do not need a large program to bring UX and CX closer together. Begin with one important journey, such as onboarding or making a first purchase. Map it end to end, invite the teams who touch it, agree on what a good experience looks like, and fix the most painful handoff first. Small, visible improvements build the case for doing the same across the rest of the customer journey.

text.content: The Psychology of Color

rich_text.plain_text: The Psychology of Color

text.content: Color psychology is the study of how colors affect human behavior and emotions. Different colors evoke different emotional responses and have cultural associations. For example, red is often associated with passion and energy, while blue represents calmness and trust. By understanding the psychological impact of colors, UX designers can strategically use them to convey specific messages and create the desired user experience.

text.content: Cultural Context and Symbolism

rich_text.plain_text: Cultural Context and Symbolism

text.content: Color symbolism can vary across different cultures and societies. For instance, in Western cultures, white is associated with purity and cleanliness, while in some Eastern cultures, it signifies mourning. When designing for a global audience, it is important to consider cultural context and ensure that color choices align with the intended message and avoid unintended associations.

text.content: Colors play a crucial role in establishing and reinforcing brand identity. For example, the use of vibrant yellow by McDonald's communicates a sense of happiness and optimism. UX designers must align the color palette with the brand's personality and values to strengthen brand recognition and create a consistent user experience.

text.content: Creating Hierarchy and Visual Cues

rich_text.plain_text: Creating Hierarchy and Visual Cues

text.content: Colors can be used to create visual hierarchy and guide users' attention. For example, a call-to-action button in a contrasting color can draw attention and encourage user interaction. Effective use of color can enhance usability, improve information hierarchy, and guide users through the desired user flow.

text.content: Building a Color System That Carries Meaning

rich_text.plain_text: Building a Color System That Carries Meaning

text.content: Color symbolism in UX works best when it is consistent. If green means success on one screen and simply decorates a button on another, users stop trusting the signal. Defining a small set of semantic colors, such as success, warning, error and information, and using them only for those purposes helps every screen speak the same language. Documenting these choices in a design system makes it easier for the whole team to apply them consistently.

text.content: Stop using Dribbble & Behance to find practical design inspiration Dribbble designs can be a great way to make practical design, but they can be problematic regarding UX concerns, as they must be practical and address actual issues. Ignore Dribbble and Behance as sources of design ideas. Check out these resources instead. As designers, we monitor the industry for emerging styles and developments. To achieve this, we frequently look to the work of other designers for guidance. Nevertheless, only some of the designs on Dribbble don’t solve UX concerns, which is one of the most significant issues with using Dribbble as a source of ideas. The designs seen on Dribbble may be lovely, but they must still be practical or even address actual issues. Our designers are responsible for producing aesthetically pleasing, practical work and effectively resolving real-world issues. Nonetheless, Dribbble tends to emphasise form over utility. As a result, you may want assistance in implementing the solutions proposed by the ideas you discover on Dribbble. Following these steps increases the likelihood that the ideas you draw upon will be suitable for solving your design problems. You may receive fresh ideas for user interface design from sites like Dribbble and Behance. Dribbble and Behance may not be ideal if you’re interested in usability, UX, and aesthetic appeal. Hence, designers should hunt for inspiration somewhere than Dribbble, namely in utilitarian designs that address real-world issues. These are some things to remember when you search for real-world design projects to inspire your own. Compliance with the UX rules in design. While brainstorming new ideas for design projects, it’s helpful to consider how those laws may be used. By studying existing designs that adhere to UX rules, you can ensure your creations are practical and easy to use. As a result of considering the user’s actions and preferences, designs that adhere to UX rules are more successful and popular. Although aesthetics play a significant role, a design’s viability depends on whether it accomplishes its intended goal (either addressing a real problem or satisfying a genuine demand). Designs that address actual needs are another critical criterion for evaluating motivation. Find challenges you’d like to solve and draw inspiration from ideas that do just that. Designs that have already undergone extensive development and consideration are also essential. To create something valuable and practical, it’s best to model it after existing designs. Looking at concept designs for ideas is beneficial, but you must also consider how the concept might function in practice.

text.content: User Experience (UX):

rich_text.plain_text: User Experience (UX):

text.content: UX encompasses the overall experience that users have when interacting with a product or service. It focuses on creating meaningful and enjoyable experiences that meet user needs and expectations.

text.content: UI refers to the visual and interactive elements of a product or service. It includes the layout, colors, typography, and interactive components that users interact with directly.

When running A/B tests, you only want to vary one element or aspect of the design—this allows you to pin-point exactly which feature influenced the result.

rich_text.plain_text: Affinity map (or affinity diagram)

text.content: An affinity map (or affinity diagram) is used by UX designers to organise their findings from qualitative user research. This entails data that can’t be counted or measured, and therefore requires thematic analysis. For example, if you interviewed five users, you might create an affinity map to cluster similar themes and topics together.

text.content: Affordances

rich_text.plain_text: Affordances

text.content: An affordance refers to all the actions that are possible with a specific object or element, depending on the user’s capabilities. For example, a cupboard has the potential to be opened but only if you can reach the handle. A car has the potential to be driven but only if you are able to open the car door, start the engine and so on. When designing digital products, the goal is to create elements whose affordances (i.e. possible actions) match the user’s expectations.

text.content: Agile UX

rich_text.plain_text: Agile UX

text.content: Agile UX is a practice that has evolved to integrate agile software development principles into the UX design process. Agile UX is all about designers and developers working collaboratively and iteratively to build and ship versions of a product in short cycles—improving and updating the product along the way. This contrasts the traditional approach of first preparing and researching at length before building anything.

text.content: (UX) Audit

rich_text.plain_text: (UX) Audit

text.content: A UX audit reviews an existing product (or an aspect of the product) to identify issues in the overall user experience. You can think of a UX audit as a user experience health check, providing you with useful data to inform future design decisions. UX audits are typically conducted for quality assurance purposes after the release of a new product or a major redesign, but companies may schedule them periodically just to keep a general pulse on the product.

rich_text.plain_text: Beta testing

text.content: Beta testing is when you launch an unfinished product to a select group of users in order to see how it performs in the real world. This allows you to identify bugs, pain points and areas of improvement for your imperfect beta product before developing and releasing it fully.

text.content: Card sorting

Card sorting is a UX research method which gives you insight into how users categorise information. In a card sorting session, participants are given notecards with different labels or topics written on them and asked to organise them in a way that feels logical. Card sorting helps you to design the information architecture (IA) of a website or app in line with user expectations. You’ll find an explanation of information architecture later on in our glossary.

text.content: Empathy map

rich_text.plain_text: Empathy map

text.content: An empathy map is a visualisation tool used by designers to depict and summarise what they know about a user (or group of users). It consists of four quadrants: “Says”, “Thinks”, “Does” and “Feels” which capture notes on what the user has said (for e.g. during an interview), what they think about a product or experience, the actions they take in a given context and how they feel during the process. As the name suggests, an empathy map helps you to build empathy for your end users

rich_text.plain_text: Design debt

text.content: Design debt (or UX debt) is the result of taking shortcuts in the design process in order to quickly reach a solution or produce a deliverable. This can lead to problems down the line and can ultimately result in a negative user experience. You might accumulate design debt if you skip user research or user testing, if you ignore style guidelines or neglect to keep adequate documentation.

text.content: Augmented reality has a more immediate application than VR since it only requires a smartphone, letting virtual objects be viewed within the real world. That low barrier is exactly why AR is creeping into everyday products faster than VR ever did.

text.content: AR in retail

text.content: AR lets customers try before they buy, reducing churn and enhancing physical and online shopping alike. Retailers like IKEA and Home Depot already use it to preview furniture and paint in real spaces.

text.content: The UX win here is confidence. One of the biggest reasons people hesitate online, or return what they bought, is uncertainty: will this sofa fit, will this shade of blue look right in my living room? Placing a true-to-scale 3D model in your own space answers that question in seconds. The same idea is spreading to eyewear, makeup and sneakers, where virtual try-ons let shoppers experiment without the trip to a store.

text.content: A Guide to Evaluating Design Projects Differentiating between objective input and subjective judgement is essential when evaluating design to pinpoint improvement areas and inform impactful design decisions. It’s essential to know the difference between constructive criticism and personal opinion when providing feedback to a designer. Providing constructive criticism requires effort. The “does it look attractive” and “does it make sense” questions are rarely sufficient. I have a history of providing constructive criticism to my coworkers and the junior designers I mentor. Knowing what aspects of your design you’d like comments on is also helpful. As I’ve mentioned, the quality of the responses you receive will increase if you provide more detail about your needs. Having someone email me a design for approval without providing any context for my input is the most annoying thing that can happen. In this piece, I’ll discuss the criteria I use to evaluate designs and why I consider them crucial. Functionality Interfaces need to serve more than one purpose when being designed. They should be logical. Those that use your creations will be doing so to fulfil a need. Usability heuristics provide a framework for UX designers to analyse their work and make improvements. A checklist is a quick and easy way to ensure all the essentials have been addressed. Knowing that your design at least considers these elements is essential to me. Usability. Is the method apparent for carrying out the desired task? What options do I have if I need to correct something? How can I know whether something I do will work or if there is an issue, even if I do it correctly? Copy. Are you using simple language that is easy to understand? How professional do you think your tone is? Could someone who wasn’t familiar with the field read it and comprehend it? Scope. Does what you’ve created fit the criteria laid out in brief? Do you have features that overcomplicate things when they aren’t necessary? Specification. When I look at your design files, how much do I learn about the inner workings of the design? Where it was necessary, have you included annotations and clarifications? Tell me about the interconnection of your various displays. Feasibility Your design must be practical if you're making something others will construct A developer needs to look at the designs you send them and be able to use them. Many designers I’ve talked to have told me that interacting with developers is a significant source of stress for them. Finding a happy medium between what we design and what is built can be challenging due to misunderstandings and competing priorities. Keeping the developers in mind while designing can help ease this pressure. Something like this is what I’m after personally: Layout. Does the layout follow a grid, and is everything in its proper place? Are the constituent parts of your layout readily identifiable? Use of a consistent style. Is there a distinct order to the fonts? Do the hues all match up with what has been established? Flexible layout. Have you specified how the design should behave when seen from various gadgets? Just where are the tipping moments, exactly? Interactions. What happens if you tap, drag, or hover over specific components? Which special effects and animations might I expect to see? If they’re not worth it, why include them? It’s more complicated to construct a workable UI; you’ll need to be familiar with the principles of how a developer thinks to do it right. If you are interested in learning more about coding, I have produced an essay that may be of assistance to you. Familiarity There needs to be more flux in terms of design norms. Although design patterns are constant, they are occasionally disrupted by novelties such as dynamic islands. And rightly so. People are resistant to change in technology. When a significant corporation changes its user interface, you should expect an avalanche of complaints. People have preexisting notions of how interfaces ought to function in their heads. What they’ve seen before has conditioned their thoughts and actions. As a user experience designer, you should cater your creations to your users’ prior knowledge and experiences. How we construct hyperlinks is an excellent illustration of how familiarity is crucial. Looking at a webpage, it should be reasonably obvious which elements can be interacted with by tapping them. You can make an educated guess, at the very least. As the underlined text is typically a clickable link, you know this is one. It doesn’t mean we can’t take some liberties with the rules. Other iterations of this pattern can arise from time to time, such as underlines that only show up when you hover. Alternatively, the text may be a contrasting colour. Yet, in general, it’s easier for people to pick up and implement your idea if you stick close to what’s already in the regulation. Flexibility As designers, finding the sweet spot where form and function coexist is our job. You’ll find examples of flawless, aesthetically pleasing user interfaces in a designer’s portfolio. Things look nice there, but that finished product will function differently. Designing a universally flawless display is impossible. Hundreds of screen sizes and resolutions can be used for tablets and PCs. It’s possible to choose from various phone models, each offering features and personalisation options. If we want as many individuals as possible to benefit from our products, we must ensure our solutions are as versatile as possible. The effectiveness of your design in the following contexts would be on my mind: Responsive. Using a mobile device against a computer at a desk. Do you use a responsive layout, or does it only function properly on a specific screen width? Translation. Would the length or width of your text blocks cause problems with the layout? Colours. What if they are colourblind or using a blue light filter? But what if they’re in dark mode? Interactions. Will someone using a keyboard be able to get around your layout quickly? Does a touchscreen require anything special to operate? Or using only one hand to gesture? Weight. If your internet speed is slow, how long will this take to load? Is there any movement or extensive photos that could bog down older or less powerful gadgets? This vast arena and I’ve barely scratched the surface here. Neither accessibility nor a responsive design expert, but I can get by. By deliberately trying to damage your designs, you may determine whether or not they are robust enough to be used successfully in various contexts. Finesse To a large extent, developing an appreciation for aesthetics is a matter of practice. To master something requires lots of time spent doing it wrong and learning from those mistakes. You can’t hasten this process. Earlier in my career as a designer, I frequently spent hours researching competing digital offerings in search of ideas. I’d re-create them to determine their secret to success, then use that knowledge in future projects. The present-day me is just as guilty of this. You can find helpful articles with general UI advice or follow industry leaders if you want more inspiration. Online, you can also find advice from numerous professionals in the design field. No amount of theory or research will replace actual hands-on experience, though. While evaluating the aesthetic quality of a design, I keep an eye out for the following details: Typography. Do the typefaces you’ve chosen complement one another? What do you think of the spacing between words? Can you identify a specific level of superiority among the styles? Consistency. Are all the pages using the same design and concept? Aesthetic. Do you find the colour scheme to be aesthetically pleasing? Do you have high-resolution images and diagrams? Careful focus on specifics. Is there symmetry and uniformity? Did you find any grammatical or spelling errors? Is there a sense of disorder or chaos in the layout? In my experience, there is no such thing as a flawless design. The more you think about your work, the more flaws you find. On the contrary, I enjoy being in that state and understanding what needs to be adjusted and why it can help you make design decisions that make a difference.

text.content: 1. Material is the metaphor

text.content: Material design is inspired by the physical world — surfaces, edges, and realistic lighting create familiar interfaces. Elements behave like sheets of paper that can stack, slide and cast shadows, so users intuitively understand how they relate to one another.

text.content: 2. Bold, graphic, intentional

text.content: 3. Motion provides meaning

text.content: 4. Adaptive design

text.content: Disposability is a tricky term to handle in the digital world. So many things are changing so quickly — programming languages, frameworks, and design trends, to name but a few — that it often feels inevitable that the things we make will be outdated almost as soon as we finish making them. This is exciting and positive in many ways, but it can also cause long-term thinking to be drowned out by short-term priorities.

text.content: The scale and speed of interface design have grown tremendously over the past few years. There are millions of mobile and web apps, and these apps can have hundreds or thousands of screens. We need design systems for large-scale design management and process optimisation. As companies worldwide continue to invest in digital transformation, they are finding that they need to reduce the time it takes to create new products. A design system is one resource that helps make this happen efficiently.  Many organizations have what they consider to be a design system, but these collections typically amount to no more than a group of elements and code snippets. While a style guide or pattern library can be a starting point for a design system, they are not the only components. Let’s dig into the fundamentals of design systems, plan how you can build and implement one in your organization, and explore several examples of organizations that are using design systems to drive success!

text.content: Ten reliable rules of thumb for UI design, covering spacing, contrast, typography, and hierarchy every designer should keep in mind.

rich_text.plain_text: Ten reliable rules of thumb for UI design, covering spacing, contrast, typography, and hierarchy every designer should keep in mind.

text.content: When in doubt, here's a list of standard practices to follow in UI design. None of these are set in stone.

rich_text.plain_text: When in doubt, here's a list of standard practices to follow in UI design. None of these are set in stone.

text.content: Treat these UI design rules of thumb as sensible defaults, then break them when a specific product gives you a good reason.

rich_text.plain_text: Treat these UI design rules of thumb as sensible defaults, then break them when a specific product gives you a good reason.

text.content: 1. Design for density, not pixels

rich_text.plain_text: 1. Design for density, not pixels

text.content: Design for the pixel density of the device, not raw pixels. A 48px button on a standard screen and a 48px button on a high-density phone are not the same physical size. Work in density-independent units (dp on Android, points on iOS) so a tap target feels the same under every thumb, whatever the screen.

rich_text.plain_text: Design for the pixel density of the device, not raw pixels. A 48px button on a standard screen and a 48px button on a high-density phone are not the same physical size. Work in density-independent units (dp on Android, points on iOS) so a tap target feels the same under every thumb, whatever the screen.

text.content: 2. Use 8dp increments

rich_text.plain_text: 2. Use 8dp increments

text.content: Spacing in increments of 8 creates consistency across devices. Most common screen sizes divide cleanly by 8, so margins, paddings and component heights stay crisp when they scale. Pick a scale (8, 16, 24, 32, 48…) and stick to it; your developers will thank you, and your layouts will stop looking "almost aligned".

Most common screen sizes divide cleanly by 8, so margins, paddings and component heights stay crisp when they scale. Pick a scale (8, 16, 24, 32, 48…) and stick to it; your developers will thank you, and your layouts will stop looking "almost aligned".

text.content: 3. Remove lines and boxes

rich_text.plain_text: 3. Remove lines and boxes

text.content: Boxes and lines dividing content could often be replaced with margin. Every divider adds visual noise the user has to read past. Try grouping related items with space first; reach for a line only when whitespace genuinely can't do the job.

rich_text.plain_text: Boxes and lines dividing content could often be replaced with margin. Every divider adds visual noise the user has to read past. Try grouping related items with space first; reach for a line only when whitespace genuinely can't do the job.

text.content: 4. Pay attention to contrast

rich_text.plain_text: 4. Pay attention to contrast

text.content: Contrast draws the user's eye and improves accessibility. Use it deliberately: high contrast for the primary action and key content, lower contrast for supporting detail. And check your text against WCAG, a light grey that looks elegant on your monitor can be unreadable on a phone in the sun.

And check your text against WCAG, a light grey that looks elegant on your monitor can be unreadable on a phone in the sun.

text.content: 5. Familiarity is good

rich_text.plain_text: 5. Familiarity is good

text.content: Be creative only within the confines of current design norms. Users spend most of their time on other products, so they arrive with expectations about where the menu lives and what a checkbox does. Break a convention only when you're sure the gain is worth the moment of confusion.

rich_text.plain_text: Be creative only within the confines of current design norms. Users spend most of their time on other products, so they arrive with expectations about where the menu lives and what a checkbox does. Break a convention only when you're sure the gain is worth the moment of confusion.

text.content: 6. Use color weight to establish hierarchy

rich_text.plain_text: 6. Use color weight to establish hierarchy

text.content: Assign different levels of importance to elements using color weight. A saturated brand color for the primary button, a softer tint for secondary actions, a neutral for everything else. If everything is bright, nothing stands out.

rich_text.plain_text: Assign different levels of importance to elements using color weight. A saturated brand color for the primary button, a softer tint for secondary actions, a neutral for everything else. If everything is bright, nothing stands out.

text.content: 7. Avoid using more than two typefaces

rich_text.plain_text: 7. Avoid using more than two typefaces

text.content: Two typefaces (with families) is usually enough. One for headings and one for body text gives you plenty of range through weights and sizes. More than that and the interface starts to feel like a ransom note.

rich_text.plain_text: Two typefaces (with families) is usually enough. One for headings and one for body text gives you plenty of range through weights and sizes. More than that and the interface starts to feel like a ransom note.

text.content: 8. Recognition, not recall

rich_text.plain_text: 8. Recognition, not recall

text.content: Minimize the user's memory load by making objects and actions visible. Show recent searches, label your icons, keep options on screen rather than hiding them behind a gesture nobody remembers. People are far better at recognizing something than remembering it.

rich_text.plain_text: Minimize the user's memory load by making objects and actions visible. Show recent searches, label your icons, keep options on screen rather than hiding them behind a gesture nobody remembers. People are far better at recognizing something than remembering it.

text.content: 9. Don't slow me down

rich_text.plain_text: 9. Don't slow me down

text.content: Be purposeful with animations; don't add unnecessary delay. Motion should explain what just happened, where a panel came from, what got deleted, not make the user wait. Keep most transitions short and snappy, and cut any animation that exists purely to look clever.

text.content: 10. Less is more

rich_text.plain_text: 10. Less is more

text.content: Every added element competes with the relevant information on a page. Before adding a badge, banner or extra button, ask what it pushes down or drowns out. The cleanest interfaces aren't the ones with the most features on screen; they're the ones where the next step is obvious.

text.content: Applying UI design rules of thumb in practice

rich_text.plain_text: Applying UI design rules of thumb in practice

text.content: Rules of thumb are most useful when they are written down and shared, not kept in one designer's head. Turn the ones your team agrees on into tokens and components: a spacing scale in 8dp steps, a short list of approved text styles, and a small set of color weights for primary, secondary and neutral elements. Once the rules live in the design system, people follow them by default instead of by memory.

Once the rules live in the design system, people follow them by default instead of by memory.

text.content: It also helps to decide in advance when a rule can bend. A dense data table may need tighter spacing than a marketing page, and a game can afford more motion than a banking app. Agree on those exceptions as a team so that breaking a rule is a deliberate choice rather than an accident.

text.content: In the vibrant realm of product design, a dynamic and sometimes funky dance takes place between fulfilling user needs and achieving your business goals. It's a delicate balance that requires finesse, creativity, and a touch of uniqueness. In this blog, we'll explore the art of harmonizing user-centric design and business objectives to create products that not only meet customer expectations but also drive success for your organization. So, put on your dancing shoes and let's groove!

text.content: Understanding the User:

rich_text.plain_text: Understanding the User:

text.content: To design a product that resonates with users, it's essential to dive deep into their world. Conduct thorough user research, engage in empathy-building exercises, and create personas to truly understand their needs, desires, and pain points. By getting into the rhythm of your users' lives, you'll gain valuable insights that can guide your design decisions and ensure that your product addresses real-world challenges.

text.content: Defining Business Goals:

rich_text.plain_text: Defining Business Goals:

text.content: Business goals

While catering to user needs is vital, it's equally important to align your product design with your business goals. What are you trying to achieve as an organization? Increased revenue, market expansion, customer retention? Identify these objectives and set measurable targets to guide your design process. Remember, your product needs to boogie to the beat of your business's long-term vision.

text.content: Finding Common Ground Between User Needs vs Business Goals:

rich_text.plain_text: Finding Common Ground Between User Needs vs Business Goals:

text.content: The tension between user needs and business goals is often smaller than it looks. Many business objectives depend on users being happy: retention comes from a product people want to return to, and referrals come from experiences worth talking about. Try mapping each business goal to the user behavior that would drive it, then ask what users need in order to behave that way. Where the two genuinely conflict, make the trade-off explicit, agree on it as a team, and decide how you will measure whether it was the right call.

text.content: Dark patterns taken a step further. Ten unethical design tactics companies use when profit comes before people, and how to spot them.

rich_text.plain_text: Dark patterns taken a step further. Ten unethical design tactics companies use when profit comes before people, and how to spot them.

text.content: I recently wrote about the 10 dark patterns that companies use to persuade their users to make decisions that favor the interest of the company rather than the individual. Asshole design takes dark patterns a step further. These aren't just sneaky interface tricks; they're business decisions designed to take more from people than they knowingly agreed to give.

text.content: Here are ten unethical UX patterns that put the business first and the person on the other side of the screen last.

text.content: 1. Shrinkflation

rich_text.plain_text: 1. Shrinkflation

text.content: Companies use this tactic to discreetly sell less of a product at the same price that it was before. The chocolate bar gets thinner, the cereal box gets more air, the subscription quietly loses a feature, but the price tag doesn't move. It relies on the fact that we rarely check the fine print on things we buy every week.

text.content: 2. Planned Obsolescence

rich_text.plain_text: 2. Planned Obsolescence

text.content: Products designed to be used for a finite amount of time, and then they're useless. Batteries that can't be replaced, software updates that slow down older devices, chargers that stop working with the next model. The product isn't broken by accident; it was built to need replacing.

text.content: 3. Lethal Enforcers

rich_text.plain_text: 3. Lethal Enforcers

text.content: Lethal enforcers require the user to take the action that the company wants before they can do what they intend to do. Create an account before you can see the price. Download the app before you can read the article. Accept the marketing emails before you can check out. The user's goal is held hostage until they give something up.

text.content: 6. Throttling

rich_text.plain_text: 6. Throttling

text.content: Throttling is when a company intentionally downgrades the service or product with the hopes that the customer upgrades. Slower speeds, longer waits, more ads on the free plan; not because it costs more to serve you, but because frustration is a sales tactic.

text.content: 7. Guilt Tripping

rich_text.plain_text: 7. Guilt Tripping

text.content: Guilt-tripping is the act of playing on one's emotions to invoke them to take a particular action. You'll know it by the opt-out buttons: "No thanks, I don't like saving money" or "I'll stay uninformed". It's shaming dressed up as copywriting.

text.content: 8. Monopoly

rich_text.plain_text: 8. Monopoly

text.content: Companies create a monopoly when they force someone to buy a currency or product that can only be used there and not transferred. In-game coins sold in bundles that never match the price of the item you want, gift cards that only work in one store, accessories that only fit one brand. Leftover value stays locked in.

Seat-back screens you can't turn off, loading screens stuffed with promotions, apps where the content is a thin strip between banners. Attention is treated as something to be harvested, not respected.

rich_text.plain_text: 10. Decoy

text.content: Companies change the terminology used to describe a word with a negative connotation. Fees become "service charges", price rises become "plan updates", tracking becomes "personalisation". The thing hasn't changed; only the label has, so it's harder to notice and harder to object to.

text.content: Designing for inclusivity means creating experiences that are adaptable, flexible, scalable, and usable by as many people as possible. There is no "average user". text.content: 1. Designing with color

rich_text.plain_text: 1. Designing with color

text.content: Maintain a 4.5:1 contrast ratio and never rely on color alone to convey information. Around 1 in 12 men has some form of color blindness, so a red error state means nothing without an icon or a message to go with it. Pair color with text, shape or position, and test your palette with a contrast checker before it ships.

Build them into your components once, and every screen benefits.

text.content: Many products started their AI journey with a single feature: a summarize button, a smart reply, a suggested tag. Those are useful, but they're increasingly just the starting point. AI is now taking on multi-step tasks, from drafting and checking a report to processing a stack of documents or running an agent that completes a job on someone's behalf.

The trouble is that it usually ends up scattered across slide decks, personal notes and old chat threads. Six months later, someone runs the same study again because nobody could find the first one.

text.content: A UX research repository fixes that. text.content: A product roadmap tells you where the product is heading, but it's only as good as the thinking behind it. text.content: Every product is used by a human brain, with all its shortcuts, limits, and habits. When a design works with those tendencies, it feels intuitive. When it works against them, people feel confused or tired without quite knowing why.

text.content: Product psychology is the practice of applying what we know about how people think and decide to the way products are designed. Used well, psychology in product design makes products easier and more satisfying. Used carelessly, it slides into manipulation. This article covers a handful of well-known principles and how to apply them responsibly.

text.content: Final thoughts

text.content: Understanding how people think is one of the most useful tools in product design. Hick's law, Fitts's law, cognitive load, social proof, and habit loops can all make your product clearer and more satisfying. Apply them with respect for the people using your product, and psychology becomes a way to help rather than persuade.

text.content: Understand where your UX organization stands.

rich_text.plain_text: Understand where your UX organization stands.

text.content: Every company does UX in some form, even if nobody calls it that. Someone decides how a screen works, how a form flows, what an error message says. What differs is how deliberately that work happens, who does it, and how much it influences decisions. A UX maturity model gives you a way to describe those differences and, more usefully, a way to see what comes next.

text.content: Several published models exist, and they use different names and numbers of stages. The details vary, but the overall shape is broadly similar. Below is a practical way to think about UX maturity, followed by how to move from one stage to the next.

text.content: The stages of UX maturity

rich_text.plain_text: The stages of UX maturity

text.content: 1. Absent

rich_text.plain_text: 1. Absent

text.content: UX isn't recognized as a discipline. Interfaces are designed by whoever is building them, usually engineers or product managers working from requirements. Nobody talks to users directly, and decisions are based on opinion or the loudest voice in the room.

rich_text.plain_text: UX isn't recognized as a discipline. Interfaces are designed by whoever is building them, usually engineers or product managers working from requirements. Nobody talks to users directly, and decisions are based on opinion or the loudest voice in the room.

text.content: 2. Emerging

rich_text.plain_text: 2. Emerging

text.content: A few people care about user experience and start doing it on their own. Maybe a designer is hired, or a developer runs a few informal usability tests. The work is valuable but fragile. It depends on individuals, has no budget, and often happens late in the process when changes are expensive.

The work is valuable but fragile. It depends on individuals, has no budget, and often happens late in the process when changes are expensive.

text.content: 3. Structured

rich_text.plain_text: 3. Structured

text.content: UX becomes a recognized function with dedicated people. There's a design process, some research happens before building, and early versions of shared patterns or a design system appear. However, UX is still often treated as a service: teams bring it in to make things look good rather than to shape what gets built.

text.content: 4. Integrated

rich_text.plain_text: 4. Integrated

text.content: UX is part of how products are planned and delivered. Designers and researchers sit in product teams from the start. Research informs roadmaps, not just screens. Leaders understand the value of UX and fund it consistently. Metrics include user-centered measures alongside business ones.

text.content: 5. User-driven

rich_text.plain_text: 5. User-driven

text.content: User understanding shapes strategy across the organization. Executives ask about user evidence before major decisions. Research insights are shared widely and reused. text.content: Retention is usually viewed in cohorts: groups of users who started in the same week or month, tracked over time. If newer cohorts retain better than older ones, your product changes are probably helping.

text.content: Most barriers in digital products aren't caused by bad intentions. They happen because inclusion gets treated as a final check rather than part of the process. By the time someone runs an audit, the structure is set, the components are built and every fix feels expensive.

text.content: Every interaction a customer has with your product either moves them toward a goal or gets in their way. text.content: Best practices for designing ethical AI systems.

rich_text.plain_text: Best practices for designing ethical AI systems.

text.content: AI systems make decisions that affect real people: what they see, what they're offered, how they're assessed and sometimes what they're denied. When those decisions go wrong, the harm isn't abstract. It lands on someone who usually had no say in how the system was built.

text.content: Responsible AI design is the practice of building these systems so they're fair, respectful of privacy and accountable for their outcomes. text.content: Good consent design is specific, timely and reversible. Ask at the moment it's relevant, explain the consequence in plain language and make it as easy to withdraw as it was to give. text.content: Growing a design team inside a large organization is a different job from doing great design work. You can have talented designers and researchers and still end up with a fragmented product, duplicated effort and teams that don't learn from each other. Enterprise UX succeeds or fails on structure: how teams are organized, how work flows between them, and how consistency holds up when dozens of squads are shipping at once.

text.content: Journey mapping is one of the simplest ways to step into your customers' shoes and stay there. text.content: Adding an AI feature to a product is easy. Getting people to understand it, rely on it and stay in control of it is much harder. Users don't trust a feature because it's clever. They trust it because it behaves predictably, explains itself when it matters and lets them step in when it gets things wrong.

text.content: That's the heart of human-centered AI: designing intelligent features around the person using them, not around the model powering them. Here are the principles that make the difference in practice.

text.content: A UI kit is a good starting point, but it's a snapshot.
